background.definition: Paget disease of the breast (PDB) is a rare dermatologic condition characterized by eczematous changes of the nipple that is often associated with an underlying carcinoma.

list.listitem: Incidence rates of PDB are reported as 0.64 episodes per 100,000 persons per year.

In a Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database cohort study from 1978 to 2014, there were 5398 patients reported with PDB - 626 (11.6%) had PD-only, 1725 (32.0%) had PD-DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ), and 3047 (56.4%) had PD-IDC (invading ductal carcinoma); in total, 88.4% of patients with PDB presented with underlying carcinoma.

Incidence of PDB with an underlying tumor decreased between 1988 and 2002 by 45%, while incidence of PDB without an underlying tumor has remained unchanged. This is possibly due to greater use of mammography as a screening test.
PDB represents 1.45% of all male breast cancers and 0.68% of all female breast cancers.
The leading theory is that PDB is caused by migration of neoplastic ductal epithelial cells to the nipple epidermis.
Two separate theories have been proposed regarding the pathophysiology of PDB.

The transformation theory states that keratinocytes in the epidermis transform into malignant Paget cells. This theory was recently supported for extramammary PD by evidence of keratinocyte-to-Paget-like cell conversion in human and mouse models, with Msi1-mTOR pathway appearing to drive keratinocyte-Paget-like cell conversion.

The epidermotropic theory, which is more widely accepted, suggests that neoplastic cells originate in the ductal epithelial cells as the result of an underlying malignancy and then migrate along the basal membrane to the nipple epidermis.
PDB is characterized by infiltration of the epidermis of the nipple by Paget cells, epithelial cells with abundant granular cytoplasm and large nucleus with prominent nucleolus.

Molecular characterization of 48 cases of PDB revealed that the HER2 subtype was most common, followed by luminal B subtype and 2 cases of the triple-negative subtype. Luminal B subtype accounts for about 40% of total breast cancers and is defined by lower expression of estrogen receptor, a low expression of progesterone receptor, and a high histologic grade.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: No clinical risk factors have been described to date. It has been assumed that risk factors are similar to those for any breast cancer.

list.listitem: USPSTF 2024 guidelines give a Grade B recommendation for biennial mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years, primarily to promote equity and not based on new evidence. For every 2000 women screened starting at age 40 instead of 50, 3 more women avoid death and gain 90 years of life at a cost of 1000 more false positives and 4 additional over-diagnosed cancers Shared decision-making should be conducted for those aged 40-50 years. No additional screening recommendations exist specifically for Paget disease of the breast (PDB).

list.listitem: Patients typically present with skin changes of the nipple that can be accompanied by other symptoms including pain, burning, itching, or nipple discharge.
Characteristic skin changes of the nipple on physical exam include erythema, ulceration, crusting, scaling, or nipple retraction.
A thorough history should identify the patient’s underlying risks for breast cancer, including personal and family history of malignancy.
Bilateral breast exam should be performed; approximately 50% of patients with PDB present with a palpable breast mass.
Lesions are almost always unilateral, with only very rare cases of bilateral involvement reported.
A lesion sparing the nipple is not likely to represent PDB.
To establish the diagnosis of PDB, a full-thickness punch or wedge biopsy of the nipple complex should be performed.
Histopathology demonstrates Paget cells in the nipple epidermis, often associated with surrounding reactive changes.
Invasive cancer associated with PD is more commonly estrogen and progesterone receptor negative and of high histologic grade.
Prior to biopsy confirmation, mammography and breast ultrasonography should be performed in patients suspected of PDB.

Characteristic mammographic changes include abnormalities of the nipple and areola, and can include underlying masses in the breast parenchyma. However, up to 50% of patients with Paget disease will have a normal mammogram.
Findings that can be seen on ultrasound include flattening or thickening of the nipple-areolar complex. The breast parenchyma can be shown to have a mass or microcalcifications.
Breast cancer can be missed on both mammography and ultrasound, with false negative rates estimated at 13%.

MRI can be used in patients with a negative mammogram and ultrasound to detect occult disease. MRI can also help with perioperative management as underlying ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) can be diagnosed.
Treatment of Paget disease is primarily dependent on the extent of underlying malignancy at presentation, with surgery being usual first-line care. C
Consider breast-conserving surgery with adjuvant radiation in patients without a palpable breast mass or evidence of extensive disease on preoperative evaluation. B

Treatment of PDB is dependent on the extent of underlying malignancy at presentation. First-line therapy is surgical (ie, mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery depending on extent of disease) with adjuvant radiation and/or chemotherapy.

Breast-conserving surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy can provide equivalent outcomes to mastectomy in patients with limited disease and with negative surgical margins according to a 2015 systematic review of 43 studies. Preoperative imaging (mammography, breast MRI) should be performed to assess extent of disease and if breast-conserving surgery is feasible.

Breast-conserving surgery (ie, central lumpectomy) is an option for women with PD alone or PD-DCIS. In a 2006 case series involving 1642 women, 293 (18%) underwent central lumpectomy, while 1349 (82%) underwent mastectomy. Fifteen-year breast-cancer-specific survival rates were 92% (95% CI, 84%-96%) with lumpectomy versus 94% (95% CI, 88%-96%) with mastectomy in women who had PD alone and women with PD-DCIS.

The finding of 10-year overall survival equivalence between breast-conserving surgery and mastectomy was also demonstrated for patients with PD-DCIS or PD-IDC using SEER data from 1973 to 2014. For both groups undergoing breast-conserving surgery, adjuvant radiation treatment improved 10-year survival.

In a 2014 meta-analysis of 7 retrospective cohort studies with 685 patients, the cumulative local recurrence rate was lower among women undergoing mastectomy than among those treated with breast-conserving surgery (5.6% versus 13.2%, p = 0.001). The analysis was limited by the fact that the studies were not randomized and did not include currently available diagnostic (MRI) and therapeutic options (radiation and tamoxifen).

A 2002 prospective cohort study of 61 women with non-invasive PDB compared cone excision with adjuvant radiation to a retrospective analysis of 33 women with cone excision alone. Five-year recurrence was 5.2% in the cone excision with radiation group versus 28.4% in the cone excision group alone (P = .0012). There was also significant difference in distant metastasis, 1.6% versus 18.2% (P = .007), and breast carcinoma death, 1.6% versus 18.2% (P = .007).

Sentinel lymph node biopsy should be considered in PDB, even without associated clinical or radiographic findings suggestive of underlying malignancy. A 2006 case series identified 39 patients with PDB, and 28% (11/39) patients had positive lymph nodes on pathology, including 11% of patients without clinical or radiographic signs of underlying disease.
In the SEER study reported above, axillary lymph node metastases were present in 20% of patients with PD-only, 3.3% of those with PD-DCIS, and 33.2% of those with PD-IDC.

Treatment of PDB in male patients primarily involves a modified radical or total mastectomy. Adjuvant radiation, chemotherapy, or hormonal therapy may be indicated based on estrogen/progesterone receptor status and presence of nodal metastasis.
Prognosis is primarily determined by the stage and grade of the underlying carcinoma of breast rather than Paget disease itself. C
Poor prognostic factors associated with PDB include estrogen and progesterone receptor negativity and HER2/neu overexpression. C
PDB is associated with more advanced breast cancer at presentation. C
PDB can occur as a local recurrence after nipple-sparing surgery for breast cancer. C
The prognosis of PDB is primarily determined by the extent of the underlying carcinoma, rather than by the Paget disease itself.

Authors of a case report and literature review found 92% to 94% 5-year survival rates for patients with PD without underlying breast carcinoma compared to 32% to 43% for those with PD an underlying palpable malignant breast tumor.

In a retrospective study of 38 patients with PDB without a palpable breast mass or mammographic density treated with local excision and post-surgical radiation, the 5-year, 10-year, and 15-year survival rate without disease was 97% for all three time periods (95% CI, 90%-100%).

Invasive cancers with associated PDB have poorer prognosis than those with equivalent stage disease without PDB. A systematic review including 3 matched cohort studies with 135 patients found that PDB was associated with ER/PR negativity and HER2/neu positivity.

Based on data from the US National Cancer Database 2004-2015, 6,864 patients with PDB were treated surgically with complete mastectomy or partial mastectomy. The 5-year survival rate after surgery was 82.5% (95% CI, 81.1%-83.9%). Factors associated with shorter survival were older age, black race/ethnicity, higher tumor grade, regional lymph node metastasis, higher cancer stage, metastatic cancer, and larger tumor size.

A retrospective cohort analysis of 32 patients with PDB matched each patient with two controls of similar age, year of treatment, and stage of breast cancer. HER2/neu overexpression occurred more often in PDB patients than in non-PDB patients (44% versus 25%, P = .008). Patients with PDB had a lower 5-year overall survival of 81.2% versus 93.8% than the non-PDB group (81.2% versus 93.8%, P = .03).

In a large retrospective cohort analysis, patients with PD-IDC were more likely to have lymph-node metastasis on presentation compared with patients with invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) alone (53% versus 34%, P < .001). Although PDB was associated with more advanced disease at presentation, when controlling for age, lymph node status, tumor size, histologic grade, type of surgery, and adjuvant therapy, PD-IDC had a risk of mortality similar to that of IDC alone (hazard ratio 0.91; 95% CI, 0.77-1.07). Those with PD-DCIS had the best prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of 97.5%.

In a review of SEER registry data from 2000 to 2013, patients with PDB alone (72.9%) and PD-IDC (71.4%) had decreased 5-year overall survival when compared with IDC alone (81.1%). This study did not include a multivariate logistic regression to account for various prognostic factors at disease presentation that may have affected overall survival, and is likely subject to lead-time bias.

A 2006 case series of the SEER registry using data from 1988 to 2002 identified the 15-year survival rate for PD-IDC at 64%, PD-DCIS at 94%, and PDB alone at 88%. Again, this must be interpreted cautiously due to the likelihood of lead-time bias, as patients with PDB are likely diagnosed at a later stage in the course of the cancer’s development.

Prognosis of PDB in male patients is worse than female patients, with 5-year survival rates of 20% to 30% in males compared with 30% to 40% in females. Similar to female patients, prognosis is primarily determined by the underlying carcinoma rather than Paget disease itself.

Risk factors for breast cancer death and recurrence in a 2008 population-based cohort of 223 women with PDB include underlying invasive cancer compared with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) (10-year breast-cancer-specific survival 75% versus 92%, P = 0.003) and a palpable tumor at presentation (10-year breast-cancer-specific survival 70% versus 87%, P = .001). Lymph-node metastasis was a risk factor for recurrence but did not show a significant difference regarding mortality.

In a follow-up cohort study of 861 patients with breast cancer who underwent nipple-sparing surgery with intraoperative radiotherapy, 36 had local recurrences (4.18%), and, among these, 7 had PD local recurrences (0.8%). The average latency period from original surgery to PD local recurrence was 32 months (range 12-49 months). Patients were treated with complete removal of the nipple areola complex and all had disease-free survival at a median follow-up of 47 months.
